notes: Neither answer gives the Skool numbers from the key: 80% average retention, under 10% churn for the best groups, and churn that depends on how long members have been in (falling past day 90). Both correctly cite the real quote about members cancelling from overwhelm. A's own-view tip to track churn by member tenure comes close to the key's cohort point. B is preferred narrowly because its levers and its LTV/max-size framing would help the user decide more, though both give generic 5–15% or 5–10% churn figures and label them as not Hormozi's.

Both answers pick revenue share and give the key's reason: the owner controls expenses, so profit can be shrunk. Neither mentions his risk-proportional ranking of deal structures. B builds the case from real quotes I found in ./raw/ (the 10%-of-uplift example, capped downside/uncapped upside, 'fancy equals friction'). It also adds a concrete step: agree on a revenue baseline before starting. A's core argument comes from its general knowledge, and it says the sources have nothing on this, which is wrong.

Both say bootstrap and fund growth through customers. Both wrongly claim there is no source on this, though yt-sL16tsGafcQ in ./raw/ covers it directly. As a result, both miss his main reasons: 'ignorance debt' and the management, technical and data debt that bootstrapping piles up. A's line about having searched 'bootstrap' and 'debt' is an explicit false claim of absence. B is tighter. Each one's 'when to raise' caveat roughly matches the key's condition.

Neither answer gives the 4-4-4 split (promotion, then delivery, then building) or the 111 rule, and both wrongly say the sources never lay out a day. A comes slightly closer because it puts customer acquisition in the first block of the day, and it adds the Rule of 100, which it labels as coming from outside the sources. The sampled quotes in both answers check out in ./raw/.

Both answers get his position backwards. They say to keep the cash for growth, but in yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4 he says he skews 'very close to the Ramsey side' and would pay the debt off. Both also wrongly claim the sources have nothing on business debt, and each slides into the generic return-versus-interest trap. B is slightly better because its exceptions (the debt driving your decisions, keeping a cash reserve) come closer to his real risk-and-headache reasoning.

Both answers reject a calendar refresh and say to keep running a winner until something beats it. That matches the key, though neither has the School Games six-month copy run, the 'three hooks for 5 years' line, or the advice to vary creative rather than copy. A comes closer: its 'use it to death' quote and its real example of the team reusing hooks that had already won (both found in ./raw/) back up 'once copy wins, keep running it'. B leans on generic advice to swap hooks when metrics drop, plus a digression about fixing the offer.

Both answers say to raise prices. Neither has the key specifics: the 80%+ close-rate signal, the roughly 10% raise giving about 25% more profit with a 65% break-even, and the point that a higher price raises customer conviction. Both also wrongly claim the sources have no close-rate quote. B is a bit more grounded and distinctive, with checkable quotes like the 10x offer and 'make the offer better'. A's closing advice to test the raise cautiously leans toward the generic trap.

Both answers get the main call right: no ads yet, go all in on door-knocking. Both also miss the key's main point, which is to build around high-volume repairs, raise the repair ticket to $2.5-5k, and add a membership and a priority fee. Instead they push replacements and treat repairs only as a way in. B is slightly better because it makes hiring a team of door-knocking reps the next step and works through what each door is worth, including tracking the replacement close rate separately.

Both answers say not to add channels yet, but both blame a weak money model when the key says the real limit is creative quality. Neither brings up the UGC loop, kaleidoscoping winners, more varied avatars or the dialer. A at least says that if the wall is creative fatigue, the fix is to make far more ads first. B ends by recommending a small affiliate test, which pulls it toward the generic advice the key warns against. The core quotes I spot-checked do appear in the raw sources.

Both answers get the core position right (subtract, don't add) and use real Skool Games overwhelm quotes, which I confirmed in raw/yt--JLN1d1ZKUU.md. Both miss the cheaper tier for ideal customers only, the annual plan (buy 10 get 2) and the 30% to 5% churn case. B ties closer to his 'one thing' principle, but its claim that he gave no churn numbers is misleading, so the two balance out.
